h1: The 6 Best Power Planter Garden Augers of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Power Planter Garden Augers: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 Power Planter garden augers scored on diameter, length, drive size and flighting, from 7-inch bulb tools to a 36-inch auger.
summary: The Power Planter 3 x 24 Inch auger is the best all-rounder, with a 1/2 inch hex drive and 10-gauge spiral flighting that suits most beds and shrubs. The 3 x 36 Inch goes deeper for bulbs and perennials, and the 7 x 28 Inch digs wide holes for shrubs. The shorter models and the grass plug tool are for narrower jobs.
intro: A garden auger is a drill bit scaled up, and the mistake most buyers make is matching it to the plant rather than to the drill. The hex size has to fit your chuck, and the drill has to survive the torque of a 7 inch bit in clay. A tool that stalls the motor is worse than hand digging.

Power Planter makes the best-known augers for this job, so this ranking compares six of its models. They are scored on diameter, length, drive size, flighting and the soils each can handle. Where a spec is not printed, the guide says so, and nothing here claims drill compatibility beyond what the hex size lists.

products.name: Power Planter 3 x 24 Inch Extended Length Auger
products.verdict: A 3 inch by 24 inch auger with a 1/2 inch hex and spiral flighting.
products.description:
This auger is 3 inches in diameter and 24 inches long, with a 1/2 inch non-slip hex drive and 10-gauge spiral flighting. It costs $25 to $50.

Twenty-four inches is the practical sweet spot. It reaches deep enough for most perennials and shrubs but stays short enough to control, and 3 inches is the diameter that most nursery pots and bulbs fit. The 10-gauge flighting is the part that carries soil out of the hole. It ranks above the 36 inch model because longer augers whip in a drill and need more arm control. It does not dig as wide as the 7 inch model.

Buy it for general bed planting. A 1/2 inch hex needs a 1/2 inch chuck, so check your drill first.
products.idealFor: General bed planting and small shrubs.
products.skipIf: You need wide holes for large plants.

products.name: Power Planter 3 x 36 Inch Bulb and Bedding Auger
products.verdict: A hand-welded 36 inch auger for deep bulbs and posts.
products.description:
Power Planter's 36 inch bulb and bedding auger is 3 inches wide, uses a 1/2 inch non-slip hex and is hand welded. It costs $50 to $100.

The extra twelve inches over the 24 inch model reach deep-planted bulbs like tulips and daffodils where depth matters. Hand welding is the build note worth noting, because a long auger works its joints harder than a short one. It ranks second because length costs control: a long bit wobbles at the tip until the hole is started, and the listing prints no flighting gauge. It beats the 12 inch Guru by reach.

Buy it for deep-set bulbs, seedlings and tall perennials. Start slow with a drill on low speed to steady the bit.
products.idealFor: Deep bulbs, tall perennials and seedlings.

products.name: Power Planter 7 x 28 Inch Extension Auger
products.verdict: A 7 inch wide auger with double flighting and replaceable blades.
products.description:
This 7 inch by 28 inch auger has double 10-gauge flighting, replaceable blades and a 1/2 inch non-slip hex. It costs $100 to $200, the highest price here.

Seven inches is the width for shrubs and one-gallon plants, a diameter the 3 inch models cannot touch. Double flighting moves more soil per revolution and replaceable blades extend the life of the tool in abrasive ground. It ranks third because the price is nearly four times the 24 inch auger and the wider bit demands real drill torque, which a light cordless drill may not deliver. It is a specialist.

Buy it for shrub and rose planting. Use a corded or high-torque drill, and keep a firm grip against kickback.
products.idealFor: Shrub, rose and one-gallon plant installs.
products.skipIf: You have a light drill or small plants.

products.name: Power Planter DIY Guru 3 x 12 Inch Garden Auger
products.verdict: A 3 by 12 inch auger for dirt, clay, rock and sand, plus paint and cement mixing.
products.description:
The DIY Guru is a 3 inch by 12 inch auger, with the listing naming dirt, clay, rocky soil and sand as suitable soils and paint and cement mixing as extra uses. It costs $25 to $50.

It is the only auger here that lists soil types and a second job. That makes it the best fit for a mixed yard where you also stir paint or mortar. At 12 inches it is short, so it cannot reach deep-planted bulbs the way the 24 and 36 inch models do. It ranks fourth for that limit, even though the price matches the 24 inch.

Buy it for shallow planting, annuals and mixing jobs. Skip it if you need depth, since 12 inches ends before a full-size bulb layer.
products.skipIf: You plant deep bulbs or tall perennials.

products.name: Power Planter Flower Planting Auger and Grass Plug Tool
products.verdict: A compact solid-steel auger for plugs, sod and hard soil.
products.description:
This is a compact flower planting auger and grass plug tool with a solid steel shaft. The listing names plugs, sod and hard soil as jobs, with paint and mortar mixing as another use. It costs $25 to $50.

Plug planting is a different job from bed digging: the hole is small and precise, and sod needs a tool that cuts a clean plug. This auger is built for that. It ranks fifth because the listing prints no diameter, length or drive size, which makes it hard to match to your drill. Against the DIY Guru, you gain plug-specific design but lose the soil list.

Buy it for lawn repair and small flower plugs. Check the drive size against your chuck before ordering.
products.idealFor: Lawn repair and small flower plugs.
products.skipIf: You want to dig bulb or shrub holes.

products.name: Power Planter 3 x 7 Inch Bulb and Bedding Auger
products.verdict: A 7 inch bulb auger on a 3/8 inch hex for compact drills.
products.description:
The 3 x 7 inch bulb and bedding auger has a 3/8 inch non-slip hex and a 5/8 inch steel shaft. It costs $25 to $50.

Its 3/8 inch drive fits small cordless drills, which makes it the only auger here that suits a light tool, and the 5/8 inch shaft adds some strength for its size. It ranks last because at 7 inches it only suits shallow bulbs and bedding plants, and the listing gives no flighting detail. It is a niche tool, though a useful one for a first-time user with a compact drill.

Buy it for crocuses, small bulbs and bedding plants. Skip it for anything deeper than a trowel's reach.
products.idealFor: Small bulbs and bedding plants with a compact drill.
products.skipIf: You need depth or wide holes.

whatMatters.detail: Diameter sets the hole width. A 3 inch bit suits bulbs, seedlings and small pots, while a 7 inch bit handles shrubs and one-gallon plants. Match the diameter to the root ball you plant. Check the listing for the stated width in inches, and not just the product name.

Length decides how deep you can plant. A 7 inch bit suits shallow bulbs, 24 inches fits most perennials, and 36 inches reaches deep. Longer bits wobble more. Choose the shortest auger that reaches the depth you need, and start the hole slowly.

The hex fits your drill chuck. The 3 x 24, 3 x 36 and 7 x 28 use 1/2 inch hexes, the 3 x 7 a 3/8 inch hex. A 1/2 inch hex needs a 1/2 inch chuck. Check your drill's chuck size and torque before buying a wide auger.

Flighting is the spiral that carries soil out of the hole. Thicker gauge resists bending, and double flighting moves more soil per turn. The 3 x 24 lists 10-gauge, the 7 x 28 double 10-gauge. Look for a stated gauge or flighting type on the listing.

Clay, rock and compacted soil stall augers, while loose loam is easy. The DIY Guru lists dirt, clay, rocky soil and sand. Rocks can jam any bit, so loosen hard ground first and run the drill slowly until the auger bites.

faq.q: What drill do I need for these augers?
faq.a: The 3 x 24, 3 x 36 and 7 x 28 use a 1/2 inch hex and need a matching chuck. The 3 x 7 uses a 3/8 inch hex for smaller drills. Wider augers need more torque, so use a corded or high-torque drill.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake with garden augers?
faq.a: Using too much speed in hard soil. A 3 x 36 or 7 x 28 can kick back if it jams on a rock. Start slowly, let the flighting bite, and keep a firm two-handed grip on the drill.

faq.q: Is the 7 x 28 worth it over the 3 x 24?
faq.a: Only for shrubs and one-gallon plants. The 7 x 28 digs 7 inch holes with double flighting but costs $100 to $200. The 3 x 24 handles bulbs and small perennials for $25 to $50.

faq.q: How do I use the grass plug tool?
faq.a: Chuck it into your drill, press it straight down into the lawn and run at low speed to cut a plug. The listing names plugs, sod and hard soil, but gives no dimensions, so check the drive size first.

faq.q: How do I clean and store an auger?
faq.a: Knock off soil, rinse the flighting and dry it before storing. The DIY Guru is also used for paint and cement mixing, so wash it promptly after those jobs to prevent hardened residue.

faq.q: Can I use one in rocky ground?
faq.a: The DIY Guru lists rocky soil, but rocks still stop any bit. Probe the area first, and if the auger jams, back it out rather than forcing it. The 7 x 28's replaceable blades help in abrasive ground.

finalTake: The Power Planter 3 x 24 Inch is the best garden auger for most gardeners because it balances reach, control and a 1/2 inch hex drive. The 3 x 36 Inch is the right call for deep bulbs, and the 7 x 28 Inch is a specialist for shrubs. The DIY Guru, the plug tool and the 3 x 7 suit narrower jobs.
